hints: Every filled digit belongs to exactly three groups: its row, its column and its 3 × 3 box. If you could remember what each group has already seen, how would you spot a repeat?
Use 27 "seen" records — 9 rows, 9 columns, 9 boxes — as boolean arrays [9][10]. The box number of cell (r, c) is (r / 3) * 3 + c / 3. Skip '.' cells; the digit is board[r][c] - '0'.

1. Create row[9][10], col[9][10], box[9][10], all false.
  2. For each cell with a digit d, compute its box b.
  3. If row[r][d], col[c][d] or box[b][d] is already true, return false.
  4. Otherwise set all three to true.
  5. After all cells, return true.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: For every filled cell, scan its whole row, column and box looking for the same digit.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: One pass over the board with 27 seen-arrays, checking and marking each digit in its row, column and box.

explain: In the first sample, every digit is marked in its row, column and box without ever finding a mark already set, so the function returns true. The second sample changes the top-left 5 into an 8. The top-left box already holds an 8 at row 2, column 2, so when the scan reaches that cell box[0][8] is already true and the function returns false (column 0 would also catch it later, at row 3). The box formula groups rows 0–2, 3–5, 6–8 and columns the same way. Remember that empty cells are the character '.' and must be skipped.
recognize: "No duplicates in any row, column or block" → one set (or boolean array) per group, check-then-mark.
